transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I... well, I came in because my mind keeps going blank at the worst times. Like, I'll look at the road-closure forms or the stop-slow paddle, and suddenly I just cannot remember the steps I've done for years. It's terrifying, honestly. Speaking of the paddle, the county issued us these new ones last month, and they're supposed to be lighter, but the grip on mine feels weird. It's like this cheap plastic that gets super slippery if it rains, which it did all last week. I had to wrap duct tape around it just to hold on, and my supervisor gave me this look, you know? But anyway, yeah, I just freeze up and can't think of what to do next.
Do you experience these memory blanks only at work or do they happen in other situations as well?

It happens... well, it happens other places, too, but work is where it scares me the most. Like I said, I'll just be looking at the road-closure forms, or holding my stop-slow paddle, and my mind just completely empties out. I suddenly can't remember the steps I've done for years. It's like someone just unplugs my brain. Speaking of unplugging, my toaster oven did that yesterday. Well, not unplugged, but it just died right in the middle of making a bagel. It's one of those fancy convection ones my sister got me for my 40th birthday last year. She always buys these expensive kitchen gadgets that I don't really need. Like, who needs an air fryer, a toaster, and a rotisserie all in one? It takes up half my counter space. And she got it in this weird mint green color that doesn't match anything else in my apartment. I tried to find the warranty for it, but I couldn't remember where I put the manual. But yeah, the blanking out... it's just really bad when I'm trying to do my job.
Do these memory blanks seem to happen when you're feeling particularly stressed or anxious?

I... I don't really know. I haven't noticed if I'm particularly anxious when it happens. I mean, the road is always stressful, I guess. Like yesterday, this woman in a white SUV was on her phone and barely slowed down. She was holding one of those giant insulated cups, you know, the ones that are super trendy right now with the handle and the straw? They hold like 40 ounces of water. I don't understand how anyone drinks that much water in a day. I try to drink more water, but it just makes me have to use the bathroom constantly, and when you're flagging on a construction site, the porta-potties are just... they're awful. Especially in the summer. They smell like chemicals and hot plastic. The site manager, Gary, he said he was going to get them cleaned twice a week, but Gary says a lot of things. He still hasn't fixed the flashing light on the barricade at the north end of the site, and I told him about that on Monday. 

But... wait, I'm sorry, what did you ask me? About the stress? Yeah, I don't know if that's what causes it. The blanking out just happens, I can't really predict it.
Do you think your mind going blank might be related to feeling overwhelmed or anxious in those moments?

I don't think it's just feeling overwhelmed, because it's not like a panic thing. It's just... like I said, my mind just goes completely blank at the absolute worst times. I'll just be staring right at the road-closure forms, or holding my stop-slow paddle, and I suddenly cannot remember the steps I've done for years. It's like the information is just gone. 

Speaking of the forms, the county just changed the font on them. They used to be in Arial, I think, but now they're in this weird serif font that's really hard to read in the sun. My supervisor, Gary—the one who won't fix the barricade light—he said it was a cost-saving measure with the printer, but how does changing a font save money? Unless it uses less ink? I buy ink for my printer at home, and it is ridiculously expensive. I have an HP DeskJet, and the cartridges cost almost as much as the printer did. I tried buying those generic refill ones online once, but they leaked all over my desk and ruined a stack of mail. One of the envelopes was a birthday card from my aunt in Florida, and it got this huge magenta stain right across the front. She always sends me a check for $25, every single year since I was a teenager, which is sweet, but... wait. What were we talking about? Oh, right, the blanking out. Yeah, it's just really scary when I'm holding the paddle and have no idea what I'm supposed to do next.
Do you feel anything physically, like a sensation in your body, when your mind goes blank?

I don't... I don't think I feel anything physical. No dizziness or heart racing or anything like that. It's really just the emptiness in my head. Like I'm just hollowed out for a second. Speaking of hollow, I was trying to carve out the center of a zucchini the other night to make those stuffed zucchini boats? I saw a video for it on Facebook. It looked so easy, but the spoon I was using kept bending. It was one of those cheap spoons from a set I bought at a dollar store years ago when I first moved into my own place. You know the ones with the really thin handles that dig into your hand? I really need to invest in some decent silverware. I saw a nice set at Target, but it was like $60, and I couldn't justify spending that much just for myself. I mostly eat frozen dinners anyway. Lean Cuisines, mostly. The mac and cheese one is okay, but the portion is so small. I always end up eating a sleeve of saltines afterward. But yeah... no, no physical feelings when the blanking happens. Just the blankness.
Do you have trouble paying attention or focusing on tasks outside of the times when your mind goes blank?

Well, I mean, it's really the blanking out that's the main problem. That's why I came in, because my mind just keeps going blank at the worst possible times. Like I said, I'll look at the road-closure forms or the stop-slow paddle and suddenly I just cannot remember the steps I've done for years. Outside of that... I don't know, maybe I get a little distracted sometimes? But it's hard to focus when it's so hot out there on the asphalt. The heat just radiates up through the soles of your boots. I buy those Dr. Scholl's inserts, the gel ones, because standing on pavement all day really does a number on your lower back. I tried telling Gary that we need better anti-fatigue mats for the stationary posts, but he just brushed me off. He said the county budget doesn't cover "luxury items." Since when is not ruining your spine a luxury? My neighbor, Carol, she works at a standing desk in an office, and her company bought everyone these really thick, squishy mats. She says it feels like standing on marshmallows. I don't really like marshmallows, though. They're too sweet, and they get stuck in your teeth. Especially the mini ones they put in hot cocoa mix. I bought a box of Swiss Miss last winter, and the marshmallows were practically dust by the time I opened the packets. But anyway, what was the question? Focus? Yeah, I guess it's mostly just the sudden blanking out that's the real issue.
Do you have trouble remembering things, like appointments or tasks, when you're not at work?

I mean, honestly, it's really just the blanking out that's the whole reason I'm here. Like I keep saying, my mind just goes completely blank at the absolute worst times. I'll be staring right at the road-closure forms, or holding the stop-slow paddle, and I suddenly cannot remember the steps I've done for years. It's just gone. Outside of work... I don't know, my memory is mostly fine, I think? I mean, I remember to feed my cat, Barnaby. He's a tabby, very vocal. He yells at me every morning at 5:30 sharp because he wants his wet food. I buy the Fancy Feast pates, the seafood ones, because he refuses to eat the chunky kind with gravy. He just licks the gravy off and leaves the meat chunks to dry out and get crusty in the bowl, which is so gross to clean up. I tried buying a cheaper brand once, Friskies, I think, and he actually knocked the bowl over and looked at me like I had insulted his ancestors. Cats are so dramatic. My cousin had a Siamese cat that would actually hide her car keys if it was mad at her. They found them in the litter box once. Can you imagine? Having to dig through kitty litter just to go to work? But, um... what did you ask? Oh, appointments. No, I usually write those on the calendar on my fridge. It's just the sudden blanking out with my work stuff that's really messing me up.
Do you have difficulty learning new things or picking up new skills outside of your job?

I don't really try to learn new things, to be honest. But I keep telling you, it's just the blanking out that's the problem. That's the whole reason I made this appointment. I'll be out there, looking at the road-closure forms or holding the stop-slow paddle, and I just suddenly cannot remember the steps I've done for years. It's like my brain just empties out. 

I did try to learn how to knit once, though. My aunt gave me all her old knitting needles when she got arthritis and couldn't do it anymore. She had this huge bag of yarn, all these crazy colors. A lot of neon green and hot pink, which I don't really wear. I prefer earth tones, you know? Like olive green or a nice mustard yellow. I bought a mustard yellow cardigan at a thrift store last fall, and it had these beautiful wooden buttons. But one of them fell off in the wash, and I couldn't find it. I think it might have gone down the drain, or maybe it's stuck in the rubber seal around the door of the washing machine. I hate doing laundry at my apartment building. The machines always smell like mildew, and someone is always leaving their wet clothes in there for hours. You have to awkwardly take their stuff out and put it on top of the dryer, and then you feel like a jerk, but what else are you supposed to do? Wait all day? I don't have time for that. I work long hours, and standing on the asphalt really drains you. 

But yeah... learning new things? I guess I haven't really tried lately. It's just the blanking out at work that's scaring me.
Do you have trouble remembering things that aren't related to your job, like what you did yesterday or what you need to pick up at the store?

I feel like a broken record here, Doc. Like I keep telling you, my memory outside of work is fine. I know what I did yesterday, and I know what I need at the store. I always write a list anyway. I need to get more of that 2% milk because whole milk really upsets my stomach. Actually, the last time I went to the Safeway down the street, they completely rearranged the dairy aisle. It took me twenty minutes just to find the butter. Why do grocery stores do that? I know they just want you to wander around and buy things you don't need, like those little baked goods they put right by the deli section in those plastic clamshells. I bought a blueberry muffin there a few weeks ago and it was so dry, it practically crumbled into dust the second I took a bite in my car. I had crumbs everywhere. I had to go vacuum my floor mats the next day. The vacuum at the car wash costs two dollars in quarters now, can you believe that? It used to be just seventy-five cents. I had to go ask the guy in the little booth to break a five-dollar bill, and he acted like I was asking him to donate a kidney. 

But anyway, what I'm trying to say is, I remember all that everyday stuff just fine. The whole reason I'm sitting in this chair right now is because of what happens when I'm on shift. My mind just completely empties out at the absolute worst times. I'll be standing there looking at the road-closure forms or holding my stop-slow paddle, and the steps I've done for literally years just vanish from my brain. It's only happening out there on the road, not when I'm trying to remember a grocery list.
Do you often feel anxious or worried when you're not at work?

I don't really feel anxious outside of work, no. I mean, I'm just living my life, you know? The only thing that really gets me worried is the blanking out. Like I keep saying, I'll be out there holding the stop-slow paddle, or staring at the road-closure forms, and I just can't remember what to do. It's terrifying because there are cars coming, you know? 

But outside of that... no, not really. I mean, I get a little stressed when my neighbor plays his music too loud. He's this college kid who moved in a few months ago, and he has this massive subwoofer that literally shakes the pictures on my wall. I have this really beautiful framed print of a lighthouse that I bought when I went to Maine a few years ago. It was supposed to be this relaxing vacation, but it rained the entire time. I ended up spending most of the trip in this tiny little antique shop just to stay dry. The owner was this older woman who collected vintage teacups. She had hundreds of them, all these delicate little floral patterns with gold rims. I almost bought one, but then I thought, when am I ever going to drink tea out of a fancy cup? I'm more of a coffee person anyway. I have a French press, but I broke the glass beaker part of it while I was washing it last week. It just slipped right out of my soapy hands and shattered in the sink. Glass everywhere. I had to use a flashlight to make sure I got all the tiny shards out of the garbage disposal. 

But anyway, no, I don't really feel anxious in general. It's just the blanking out on the job that's really got me worried.
Do you think that when your mind goes blank, it might be a way for you to momentarily escape or cope with the stress of being in a potentially dangerous situation, like directing traffic?

Escape the stress? No, I don't think it's some kind of subconscious escape trick. Like I've been trying to tell you, it's not me zoning out on purpose. I literally came in here because my mind just keeps going blank at the absolute worst times, and it's out of my control. I'll be staring right at the stop-slow paddle, or looking down at the road-closure forms, and it's like someone just wiped my brain completely clean. I suddenly cannot remember the steps I've done for years. It's not a coping thing, it's terrifying! 

I mean, sure, it is dangerous out there, and people do not pay attention. Just last Tuesday there was this guy in a giant silver pickup truck—one of those lifted ones with the huge tires? He was eating a bowl of cereal while driving. A literal ceramic bowl with a metal spoon. Who does that? What if he had to slam on the brakes? Milk would go everywhere. That actually reminds me of when my sister tried to eat soup in my Honda Civic back in college and spilled tomato bisque all over the passenger seat. We tried absolutely everything to get the stain out. Baking soda, club soda, that expensive upholstery foam in the yellow can with the plastic brush attached to the lid. The brush bristles were so stiff they actually snagged the fabric, so then I had a stained *and* fuzzy seat. I was so mad at her. I ended up just buying a cheap seat cover from AutoZone to hide it. It came in a pack with a steering wheel cover that matched, like a black and gray mesh pattern, but those things get so incredibly hot in the summer. Have you ever burned your hands on a steering wheel? It's the worst. You have to drive with just your fingertips for the first ten minutes with the AC blasting. 

But no, I'm not trying to escape anything. My brain is just failing me out there with the paddle and the forms, and I don't know why.
Do you ever find yourself unable to remember what to do next in hobbies or other activities that require your full attention?

No, not with hobbies at all. Doc, I feel like we're going in circles here. Like I've been saying over and over, the whole reason I came in to see you is because my mind just totally empties out only when I'm out there on the job. I'll be looking right at my stop-slow paddle or trying to fill out the road-closure forms, and the steps I've known how to do for years just completely vanish from my head. It's just at work. 

With my hobbies, my focus is perfectly fine. I actually do a lot of cross-stitch, which takes a ton of concentration. I'm working on this huge pattern right now of a Victorian house, and it has all these tiny little French knots for the flowers in the front yard. I had to buy this special magnifying lamp just to see what I'm doing because the embroidery floss is so thin. I ordered it online, and when it arrived, the box was completely crushed on one side. The delivery driver just left it right on my porch in the pouring rain and didn't even bother to ring the doorbell. I have one of those video doorbells, you know? But the battery died last week because I forgot to charge it. You have to take the whole faceplate off with this tiny little star-shaped screwdriver that I always lose in my junk drawer. 

My junk drawer is an absolute disaster right now, to be honest. It's just full of soy sauce packets from Chinese takeout and dead AA batteries. Why do we always keep dead batteries? It makes no sense. I should just throw them away, but then I always think, what if they still have a little bit of juice left for the TV remote? My remote has that down-arrow button that always gets stuck, so half the time I end up scrolling way past the channel I actually want to watch anyway. I was trying to watch that baking show the other night, the one where they have to make the giant sculptures out of chocolate? It's amazing how they get the chocolate to balance like that without melting under the studio lights. 

But anyway, to answer your question, no. I never forget what I'm doing with my cross-stitch or anything else. It's literally just the paddle and the forms on the road where my brain decides to wipe itself clean.
Do you ever have moments where you can't remember what to do next in situations outside of work that are particularly high-pressure or stressful?

High-pressure situations outside of work? No, not really. Doc, I feel like a broken record here. I don't know how else to explain it to you. I came in because my mind keeps going blank at the absolute worst times *at work*. It's only when I look at the road-closure forms or I'm holding the stop-slow paddle, and then suddenly I just cannot remember the steps I've done for literally years. It's like a switch flips and it's all gone. 

If I'm in a stressful situation at home, I handle it perfectly fine. Like last month, I had to do my taxes, which is always super high-pressure for me because I'm terrified of getting audited. I use that online software, but my laptop is so old the fan sounds like a jet engine taking off. It gets so hot it actually warped the fake wood veneer on my coffee table. I was so upset because I bought that table at a garage sale for like, fifteen dollars, and it was in perfect condition. The woman selling it was moving to Florida to be closer to her grandkids. She had this massive collection of ceramic frogs she was trying to get rid of, too. I didn't buy any, though. Frogs kind of creep me out ever since I stepped on one barefoot when I was a kid. It was so squishy. 

We used to live near this creek, and the mosquitoes were just awful in the summer. My mom used to make us spray this horrible-smelling bug repellent that had DEET in it, and the wind would always blow it right into my mouth. It tasted like bitter, poisonous chemicals. I can still taste it if I think about it too hard. Have you ever accidentally tasted aerosol bug spray? It completely ruins your whole day. You can drink a gallon of water and the taste just coats the back of your throat. 

But anyway, no, my brain doesn't blank out during taxes or emergencies or anything like that. I know exactly what to do. It's just the forms and the paddle. That's the whole reason I'm here.
Do you ever have moments where you can't remember what to do next in situations outside of work that are particularly high-pressure or stressful?

Wait, didn't you just ask me that exact same thing? I swear we just talked about this. Like I just said, no, outside of work I handle stress completely fine. I only came in here because my mind keeps going blank at the absolute worst times when I'm on the job. I'll be staring right at the stop-slow paddle or the road-closure forms, and I suddenly cannot remember the steps I've done for years. It just completely empties out. 

But at home? If there's an emergency, I know exactly what to do. Like when my washing machine hose burst a few weeks ago. Water was gushing everywhere, all over the linoleum, and I didn't freeze up or blank out at all. I just marched right behind the machine and cranked the shut-off valve. Though, honestly, that valve was so rusted it took both hands and all my body weight to turn it. I really need to get a plumber out to look at the pipes, but they charge so much just to pull into your driveway. 

My neighbor, Gary, said he knew a guy who could do it for cheap, but Gary is the same guy who tried to fix his own roof with duct tape and a blue plastic tarp. It looked absolutely ridiculous. The wind caught it during that huge storm we had back in October, and it blew right into my elm tree. I love that tree, it turns this beautiful golden yellow in the fall, but the leaves get absolutely everywhere. You have to rake them like every three days or they completely smother the grass. I actually bought one of those electric leaf blowers to make it easier, but the cord is never quite long enough to reach the edge of the driveway near the mailbox. So I always have to drag out this heavy-duty orange extension cord, and it tangles if you even look at it wrong. I spend more time untangling the cord than I do actually blowing the leaves. 

But yeah, I don't blank out when stuff like that happens. It's only the paddle and the forms at work.
Do you think that when your mind goes blank, it might be a way for you to disconnect from what's happening around you?

Disconnect from what's happening? No, I don't think it's some deep psychological thing where I'm trying to escape. Like I've been trying to tell you this whole time, I only came in because my mind keeps going blank at the absolute worst times. I'll just be standing there looking at the road-closure forms, or holding the stop-slow paddle, and I suddenly cannot remember the steps I've done for years. It's not me disconnecting, the information is just gone. 

Speaking of those forms, though, they still use that awful carbon copy paper. I didn't even know they still manufactured that stuff, but it gets this weird blue smudge all over the side of my hand. You can't even wash it off with regular soap. I have to use that gritty orange pumice soap that mechanics use. My dad used to keep a huge jug of that in our garage when I was growing up because he was always tinkering with his old Chevy Nova. He loved that car, but the alternator was constantly dying on it. He'd spend every Sunday underneath it, just cursing at the engine. We always had Sunday dinner at like eight o'clock at night because he refused to come inside until he fixed whatever was rattling. My mom would make this incredible pot roast with carrots and potatoes, but by the time we ate it, the potatoes were always super mushy from sitting in the slow cooker too long. I actually kind of like mushy potatoes, though, especially if you mash them up into the gravy. 

But anyway, no, I'm not trying to disconnect or zone out. It's literally just my brain wiping the slate clean when I'm trying to do my job.
Do you feel like you're still aware of your surroundings when your mind goes blank?

Am I aware? Yeah, of course I am. I see the street, I hear the traffic. It's not like I pass out or go blind. But like I've been saying this whole time, I came in because my mind keeps going blank at the absolute worst times. I'll be looking right at the road-closure forms or holding the stop-slow paddle, and I suddenly just cannot remember the steps I've done for years. The steps are completely gone, but I still see everything else around me. 

Like, right when it happened on Tuesday, I remember I was staring at this bright yellow Volkswagen Beetle that was first in line at my crosswalk. You really don't see those much anymore. My aunt Brenda used to drive a yellow Beetle back in the nineties, and it had that little built-in flower vase on the dashboard. She always kept a fake plastic daisy in it. Her car always smelled like a mix of stale cigarette smoke and vanilla air freshener, because she smoked those long, skinny Virginia Slims. I always thought the boxes looked so fancy when I was a kid, almost like little purses. She used to let me keep the empty boxes, and I would store my Polly Pockets in them. Do you remember Polly Pockets? The original ones, I mean, not the big ones they make now. They were so tiny, I was always losing the little rubber clothes in the shag carpet in my bedroom. My mom hated that carpet because the vacuum cleaner brush would always get jammed on the long fibers. We had to take the vacuum to the repair shop by the strip mall like three times a year. The guy who fixed them always wore these thick suspenders with tape measures printed on them. 

But yeah, I'm totally aware of my surroundings when it happens. It's just the steps for my job that completely disappear from my brain.
Do you feel like you're observing yourself from outside your body when your mind goes blank?

Outside my body? No, definitely not. I'm right there in my boots. I'm just standing there, but like I've told you, I only came in because my mind keeps going blank at the absolute worst times. I'll be holding the stop-slow paddle, looking right at the road-closure forms, and I suddenly cannot remember the steps I've done for years. I'm fully in my body, my brain is just empty. 

Speaking of my boots, though, I really need to get a new pair. The soles are wearing down on the left side, which is weird because I'm right-handed. I guess I must lean on my left foot when I'm standing for a long time. I bought them at that surplus store out on Route 9, the one with the giant inflatable gorilla on the roof. They put him up for a Memorial Day sale like five years ago and just never took him down. He looks so sad now, kind of deflated and faded from the sun. The sun is brutal out there on the pavement, too. I have to wear SPF 50 every single day, even in the winter, or I get these terrible freckles on my nose. My sister gets them too, but she says they're "sun kisses" and thinks they're cute. She's always been like that, trying to find the bright side of everything. She even made a scrapbook when her basement flooded. She took pictures of all the ruined boxes and put little stickers of rain clouds next to them. I could never do that. If my basement flooded, I'd probably just sit on the stairs and cry. 

But no, I don't feel like I'm floating or watching myself or anything weird like that. I'm just standing there, not knowing what to do with the paddle.
Do you ever feel like you're in a daze or disconnected from what's happening around you when your mind goes blank?

Disconnected? No, I wouldn't say I'm in a daze. I mean, I'm fully awake and everything. But like I keep trying to explain, I only came in because my mind keeps going blank at the absolute worst times. I'll be looking right at the road-closure forms or holding the stop-slow paddle, and I suddenly cannot remember the steps I've done for years. I'm not in a daze, the information just completely vanishes. 

It's really frustrating, especially when it's hot out. The heat shimmering off the asphalt makes everything look kind of wavy anyway. Sometimes I wish I worked indoors, like at a bakery or something. The smell of fresh bread is just the best thing in the world. There's this little panaderia near my apartment that makes these incredible conchas. They have the pink and yellow sugary tops, and they're so soft inside. I used to go there every Saturday morning with my ex-boyfriend, Mark. Mark was obsessed with those pastries. He was a good guy, mostly, but he had this weird habit of collecting vintage soda cans. Our whole apartment was lined with them. He had this one Billy Beer can from the seventies that he treated like it was made of solid gold. He actually bought a little glass display case for it, the kind you'd see in a jewelry store. It had a tiny spotlight and everything. I always thought it was so silly to care that much about an empty can of terrible beer, but he said it was history. We broke up because he wanted to move to Ohio to be closer to his brother, and I just couldn't see myself living in Ohio. I don't know why, it just seems so flat. 

But no, I don't feel like I'm in a daze or anything. My brain just turns off when I need it the most.
Do you feel like you're spacing out or disconnecting from reality when your mind goes blank at work?

Spacing out? No, I'm not spacing out. I know exactly what's real. But like I keep telling you, I only came in because my mind keeps going blank at the absolute worst times. I'll be holding the stop-slow paddle, looking right at the road-closure forms, and I suddenly cannot remember the steps I've done for years. I'm definitely in reality, the reality is just that my brain empties out the instructions. 

And reality is very loud out there on the road anyway, so you can't really disconnect from it. Especially with the dump trucks. There's this one local hauling company, and all their trucks are painted this blinding neon green color. It's exactly the same color as this slime toy I had when I was a kid in the eighties. It came in a little plastic miniature trash can, do you remember those? I loved that stuff until I accidentally left it on the radiator in the hallway and it melted all down into the metal grates. My dad was so incredibly mad. He spent like three hours scraping the dried slime off with a metal putty knife. He was always fixing things, though. He had this massive wooden workbench in the garage, and he kept all his screws and nails sorted in old glass baby food jars. My mom saved dozens of them when my younger brother was a baby. He went through so many jars of those mashed peas, which is hilarious because now he refuses to eat anything green. He won't touch a vegetable to save his life. He actually insisted on having a steak-only menu at his wedding reception. No salad, just meat and potatoes. His wife was furious about the catering bill, but her dress was absolutely gorgeous. It had these long lace sleeves that looked like something out of a vintage magazine. 

But anyway, no, I'm not spacing out or losing touch with reality. I just literally forget how to do my job out of nowhere.
Is there something specific that happens right before your mind goes blank, like a noise, a person, or a particular task?

A noise? I mean, it's a construction zone, there's always noise. The backup beepers on the loaders are probably the worst. It's this constant, high-pitched sound. It actually sounds exactly like the alarm clock I had in college. I shared a tiny dorm with this girl named Sarah, and she would hit snooze like ten times every single morning. She was a theater major and always had these crazy late rehearsals, so she was always exhausted. She played a tree once in some Shakespeare play, and she was so mad about it because she wanted the lead role. She actually glued real leaves and twigs to her tights for the costume, and she ended up bringing all these little spiders into our room. We had to call maintenance to spray the baseboards. The maintenance guy was really sweet, though. He gave us a coupon for a pizza place downtown, but their crust tasted exactly like cardboard. I don't know how they stayed in business. They had these red checkered tablecloths that were always sticky, no matter how much they wiped them down. 

But anyway, no, there isn't a specific trigger or a certain person or anything like that. Like I feel like I've been saying this whole time, it just happens out of nowhere. I'll just be staring right at my stop-slow paddle or looking down at the road-closure forms, and my mind just completely empties out. All the steps I've known how to do for years just vanish, and I'm left with absolutely nothing in my head.

patient.answer:
Outside my body? No, definitely not. I'm right there in my boots. I'm just standing there, but like I've told you, I only came in because my mind keeps going blank at the absolute worst times. I'll be holding the stop-slow paddle, looking right at the road-closure forms, and I suddenly cannot remember the steps I've done for years. I'm fully in my body, my brain is just empty. 

Speaking of my boots, though, I really need to get a new pair. The soles are wearing down on the left side, which is weird because I'm right-handed. I guess I must lean on my left foot when I'm standing for a long time. I bought them at that surplus store out on Route 9, the one with the giant inflatable gorilla on the roof. They put him up for a Memorial Day sale like five years ago and just never took him down. He looks so sad now, kind of deflated and faded from the sun. The sun is brutal out there on the pavement, too. I have to wear SPF 50 every single day, even in the winter, or I get these terrible freckles on my nose. My sister gets them too, but she says they're "sun kisses" and thinks they're cute. She's always been like that, trying to find the bright side of everything. She even made a scrapbook when her basement flooded. She took pictures of all the ruined boxes and put little stickers of rain clouds next to them. I could never do that. If my basement flooded, I'd probably just sit on the stairs and cry. 

But no, I don't feel like I'm floating or watching myself or anything weird like that. I'm just standing there, not knowing what to do with the paddle.

doctor.question: Do you ever feel like you're in a daze or disconnected from what's happening around you when your mind goes blank?

patient.answer:
Disconnected? No, I wouldn't say I'm in a daze. I mean, I'm fully awake and everything. But like I keep trying to explain, I only came in because my mind keeps going blank at the absolute worst times. I'll be looking right at the road-closure forms or holding the stop-slow paddle, and I suddenly cannot remember the steps I've done for years. I'm not in a daze, the information just completely vanishes. 

It's really frustrating, especially when it's hot out. The heat shimmering off the asphalt makes everything look kind of wavy anyway. Sometimes I wish I worked indoors, like at a bakery or something. The smell of fresh bread is just the best thing in the world. There's this little panaderia near my apartment that makes these incredible conchas. They have the pink and yellow sugary tops, and they're so soft inside. I used to go there every Saturday morning with my ex-boyfriend, Mark. Mark was obsessed with those pastries. He was a good guy, mostly, but he had this weird habit of collecting vintage soda cans. Our whole apartment was lined with them. He had this one Billy Beer can from the seventies that he treated like it was made of solid gold. He actually bought a little glass display case for it, the kind you'd see in a jewelry store. It had a tiny spotlight and everything. I always thought it was so silly to care that much about an empty can of terrible beer, but he said it was history. We broke up because he wanted to move to Ohio to be closer to his brother, and I just couldn't see myself living in Ohio. I don't know why, it just seems so flat. 

But no, I don't feel like I'm in a daze or anything. My brain just turns off when I need it the most.

doctor.intent: Determine if patient experiences memory blanks due to dissociation
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're spacing out or disconnecting from reality when your mind goes blank at work?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about dissociative symptoms, such as spacing out or disconnecting from reality (derealization/depersonalization), which are not covered by any of the items in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Spacing out? No, I'm not spacing out. I know exactly what's real. But like I keep telling you, I only came in because my mind keeps going blank at the absolute worst times. I'll be holding the stop-slow paddle, looking right at the road-closure forms, and I suddenly cannot remember the steps I've done for years. I'm definitely in reality, the reality is just that my brain empties out the instructions. 

And reality is very loud out there on the road anyway, so you can't really disconnect from it. Especially with the dump trucks. There's this one local hauling company, and all their trucks are painted this blinding neon green color. It's exactly the same color as this slime toy I had when I was a kid in the eighties. It came in a little plastic miniature trash can, do you remember those? I loved that stuff until I accidentally left it on the radiator in the hallway and it melted all down into the metal grates. My dad was so incredibly mad. He spent like three hours scraping the dried slime off with a metal putty knife. He was always fixing things, though. He had this massive wooden workbench in the garage, and he kept all his screws and nails sorted in old glass baby food jars. My mom saved dozens of them when my younger brother was a baby. He went through so many jars of those mashed peas, which is hilarious because now he refuses to eat anything green. He won't touch a vegetable to save his life. He actually insisted on having a steak-only menu at his wedding reception. No salad, just meat and potatoes. His wife was furious about the catering bill, but her dress was absolutely gorgeous. It had these long lace sleeves that looked like something out of a vintage magazine. 

But anyway, no, I'm not spacing out or losing touch with reality. I just literally forget how to do my job out of nowhere.

patient.answer:
A noise? I mean, it's a construction zone, there's always noise. The backup beepers on the loaders are probably the worst. It's this constant, high-pitched sound. It actually sounds exactly like the alarm clock I had in college. I shared a tiny dorm with this girl named Sarah, and she would hit snooze like ten times every single morning. She was a theater major and always had these crazy late rehearsals, so she was always exhausted. She played a tree once in some Shakespeare play, and she was so mad about it because she wanted the lead role. She actually glued real leaves and twigs to her tights for the costume, and she ended up bringing all these little spiders into our room. We had to call maintenance to spray the baseboards. The maintenance guy was really sweet, though. He gave us a coupon for a pizza place downtown, but their crust tasted exactly like cardboard. I don't know how they stayed in business. They had these red checkered tablecloths that were always sticky, no matter how much they wiped them down. 

But anyway, no, there isn't a specific trigger or a certain person or anything like that. Like I feel like I've been saying this whole time, it just happens out of nowhere. I'll just be staring right at my stop-slow paddle or looking down at the road-closure forms, and my mind just completely empties out. All the steps I've known how to do for years just vanish, and I'm left with absolutely nothing in my head.
